analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a government-run Medicare-for-all program covering everyone.
analysis.headline: Despite 77 cosponsors, all Democrats, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a single public health plan covering every U.S. resident, with no deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance, paying for care with a mix of existing health spending and new taxes on high earners, payroll income, and stock and bond trades. Private insurers would have been barred from selling coverage that duplicates the public plan, and investor-owned hospitals would have had to convert to nonprofit status. It was referred to three House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would get comprehensive coverage — including dental, vision, hearing, mental health, long-term care, and prescription drugs — with no out-of-pocket costs at the point of care, and free choice of participating doctors and hospitals. The roughly 49 million uninsured Americans at the time, and anyone whose insurance denied care or imposed large deductibles, would benefit most. Displaced insurance clerical workers would get two years of salary-parity transition benefits and first priority in retraining.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees all medically necessary care to every U.S. resident — including primary care, hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care — with no deductibles, copayments, or other cost-sharing.
Gives patients free choice of any participating physician or hospital anywhere in the country, with benefits portable across state lines.

Finances the program by redirecting what the government already spends on Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP, plus new progressive taxes on the top 5% of earners, payroll income, unearned income, and stock and bond transactions.
Provides two years of salary-parity transition benefits (up to $100,000 a year) and first priority in retraining for insurance and billing workers whose jobs are eliminated.

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income households pay through increased income taxes on the top 5% of earners; employers and workers pay through a progressive payroll and self-employment tax; investors pay through new taxes on unearned income and on stock and bond trades. Private health insurers lose their core business, and owners of investor-owned hospitals are compensated over 15 years for converting to nonprofit status.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, payroll taxpayers, and investors

drawbacks.text: The new taxes are real and large: higher income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a payroll and self-employment tax, a tax on unearned income, and a tax on stock and bond transactions, on top of existing government health spending.

The bill outlaws private insurance that duplicates the public plan, eliminating the private health insurance industry as it exists and the jobs that go with it, and requires investor-owned hospitals to convert to nonprofits, with owner losses paid off over 15 years through Treasury bonds.

Payment to doctors and hospitals would be set through government-negotiated fee schedules and annual global budgets, which could pay providers less than private insurers do and concentrates pricing power in a federal director.

Funding assumes large savings from reduced paperwork and bulk drug procurement; if those savings fell short, the bill authorizes unlimited additional annual appropriations, leaving the program's cost open-ended.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the entire private insurance model for a single public plan: everyone gets comprehensive care with no out-of-pocket costs, paid for by redirecting existing health programs and raising taxes on high earners, payroll income, and financial trades. The gains — universal coverage, no deductibles, and negotiated drug prices — are large and fall on ordinary households; the costs are the new taxes, the end of private duplicative coverage, and the risk that government-set budgets underpay providers or underfund care. Whether bulk-buying and paperwork savings covered the gap was untested; the bill's own answer was to authorize unlimited supplemental appropriations.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced, bounced among subcommittees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers of Michigan introduced the bill on February 11, 2011, with 25 original cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources — splitting it among panels rather than sending it to one.
Within days it was sent to subcommittees: the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce on February 14 and 18, and the Subcommittee on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs on February 16.
No further action of any kind was taken; the bill accumulated 77 cosponsors, all Democrats, and expired with the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and investor-owned hospital companies were better off, since the bill would have barred duplicative private coverage and forced for-profit providers to convert to nonprofits. High earners and investors also avoided the new income, payroll, and financial-transaction taxes. No one who supported the bill got so much as a committee hearing.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 25 original cosponsors, then gathered 77 total over the Congress.

for.name: 77 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to their committees.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to three committees and never brought it to the floor in two years.

against.name: Private health insurance industry
against.role: Health insurers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Fought single-payer proposals as a threat to their core business, which the bill would have eliminated by barring duplicative coverage.

sides.party_line_note: All 77 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; the Republican majority controlled the committees and never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to sell coverage duplicating the public plan, ending the industry's core product; insurers could sell only non-medical-necessary add-ons like cosmetic surgery coverage. Its profit model depends on standing between patients and care, which the public plan removes.

industries.industry: Investor-owned hospitals and for-profit care providers
industries.note: Only public or nonprofit institutions could participate; for-profits would have to convert to nonprofit status, with owners compensated for losses over 15 years via Treasury bonds. Converting to nonprofit care delivery shifts resources from shareholder returns to patient care.

The program would negotiate drug prices annually and run a formulary promoting generics, ending the industry's ability to set US prices market by market. Cheaper negotiated drugs lower costs for everyone in the plan.

industries.industry: Health insurance billing and administrative workers
industries.note: Jobs tied to insurance paperwork would be eliminated, but the bill guarantees two years of salary-parity transition benefits and first priority in retraining, so the direct hit to these workers is buffered.

industries.industry: Nonprofit HMOs delivering their own care
industries.note: Nonprofit HMOs that employ salaried clinicians in their own facilities are explicitly allowed to participate and receive global budgets or capitation payments, locking in a favored role for staff-model nonprofits.
